SOURCE:
American Academy of Dermatology - Basal Cell Carcinoma
https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/basal-cell-carcinoma

Basal cell carcinoma is a type of skin cancer that commonly grows slowly.
It can appear in different forms including a firm raised growth, a scaly
spot or patch, a sore that does not heal or repeatedly returns, a new mark
that resembles a scar, or shiny bumps.

A lesion that grows, bleeds, crusts, repeatedly breaks open, or does not heal
should be evaluated by a dermatologist.

Ultraviolet radiation from sunlight and indoor tanning devices is an important
risk factor for basal cell carcinoma.

People of all skin colors can develop basal cell carcinoma.

A visual image alone cannot establish that a lesion is basal cell carcinoma.
Professional clinical evaluation is required for diagnosis.

A dermatologist can determine whether a suspicious lesion requires further
evaluation. When skin cancer is suspected, biopsy may be required to establish
a definitive diagnosis.

SOURCE:
American Academy of Dermatology - How to Find Skin Cancer
https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/find

New, changing, different, itching, or bleeding spots on the skin should
receive appropriate professional evaluation.

Skin cancer can occur in people of different skin colors.

Self-examination can help people notice new or changing lesions, but
self-examination and photographs cannot establish a definitive diagnosis.

A dermatologist is the appropriate specialist for evaluation of suspicious
skin lesions.

When skin cancer is suspected, biopsy and microscopic examination may be
needed to determine whether cancer cells are present.

Skin protection from ultraviolet radiation is an important preventive measure.

SOURCE:
American Academy of Dermatology - Melanoma Signs and Symptoms
https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/skin-cancer/types/common/melanoma/symptoms

Melanoma can appear as a new or changing spot or mole.

Important warning signs include:
A - Asymmetry: one half of a spot does not match the other half.
B - Border: the border may be irregular, scalloped, or poorly defined.
C - Color: the spot may contain multiple colors.
D - Diameter: melanomas are often larger than 6 mm when diagnosed, but
smaller lesions can also occur.
E - Evolving: the spot changes in size, shape, color, or appearance.

A spot that looks different from other spots, changes, itches, bleeds,
or becomes painful should be evaluated by a dermatologist.

Melanoma can occur on different parts of the body, including areas that
receive little sun exposure.

The ABCDE features are warning signs and do not establish a diagnosis.

A dermatologist should evaluate suspicious lesions. A skin biopsy is used
when needed to establish a definitive diagnosis.
